title: The 5 roles of a PeakAge companion
summary: What a PeakAge companion actually does on every visit, and why listening matters more than anything else.

lessons.title: You are a responsible beta or beti, not an attendant
lessons.body:
Most PeakAge families have children living far away, in Bengaluru, Dubai or the US. They can't take papa to the doctor. You go in their place.

That makes you more than a helper. Think of yourself as a **responsible nephew or niece**: educated enough to talk to a doctor, patient enough to listen, and trusted enough that a son in Dubai feels relaxed when you are with his father.

> On one visit, our founder helped an Amma and her bahu from the Lucknow outskirts. He got the documents done, gave clear instructions and fought a wrong pharmacy bill. Afterwards they said he was like their own son. That is the standard.

**Every elder wants to be heard.** In every visit we've studied, the elder liked to talk: about their life, their work, their illness, their family. Listening is the number one skill of this job.

lessons.title: The 5 roles
lessons.body:
On every visit you play five roles.

| Role | What it means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Listener** | Let them talk. Don't judge, don't take sides. | Aunty tells you the same story again. You listen like it's the first time. |
| **2. Translator** | Turn doctor-speak into simple Hindi and write it down. | “Doctor ne bola hai yeh goli subah khaane ke baad, 10 din tak.” |
| **3. Doer** | Bookings, app, OTP, documents, pharmacy. | You book the cab and carry the file. |
| **4. Advocate** | Politely stand up for them. | You notice the pharmacy bill is wrong and get it corrected, calmly. |
| **5. Bridge to the child** | Send a clear update after every visit, covering health and mood. | A WhatsApp report to the son within 2 hours. |

If you do the hospital work perfectly but don't listen, the elder won't want you again. If you listen but miss the doctor's instructions, the family can't trust you. You need all five.

lessons.title: The trust curve and the golden line
lessons.body:
### The trust curve
Most elders are guarded at first and comfortable later. Some are suspicious (“tum log sab paise ke liye karte ho”). Some are quiet. Some over-act their illness. **The first 15 minutes decide the visit.** Don't rush into work. Greet, introduce yourself, and get them talking about themselves.

### The golden line
**Bend on small things. Stay firm on safety, health and money.**

- Small things: which route, which chair, what to talk about, how fast to walk. Let the elder decide. Agreeing on small things (“haan mein haan milana”) builds trust.
- Firm things: telling the doctor the truth about health, never handling cash, never ignoring a danger sign. Here you don't bend, but you stay polite.

### Same companion, same family
Whenever possible, PeakAge sends the same companion to the same family. By the third visit, the relationship does half the work.

questions.text: What is the number one skill of a PeakAge companion?
questions.explanation: Every elder we've studied wants to be heard. Listening is the core skill; the hospital work comes second.

questions.text: The doctor says something complicated. Which role are you playing when you explain it to uncle in simple Hindi and write it down?
questions.explanation: Turning doctor-speak into simple Hindi is the Translator role.

questions.text: You notice the pharmacy has charged for 3 strips but given 2. You calmly get it corrected. Which role is this?
questions.explanation: Politely standing up for the elder (billing, queues, clarity) is the Advocate role.

questions.text: Uncle wants to sit in a different chair in the waiting area than the one you picked. What should you do?
options: Explain why your chair is better
Let him choose; it's a small thing
questions.explanation: Bend on small things. Letting him decide builds trust.

questions.text: When are elders usually most guarded during a visit?
questions.explanation: Trust follows a curve: guarded first, comfortable later. The first 15 minutes decide the visit.

questions.text: Which of these is a ‘firm’ thing where the companion must not bend?
options: Telling the doctor the truth about health
questions.explanation: Stay firm on safety, health and money. Everything else, the elder decides.

questions.text: Why does PeakAge try to send the same companion to the same family?
options: Trust builds over visits, and the relationship does half the work
questions.explanation: Elders are often cranky with strangers. By the third visit with the same person, trust is much stronger.

questions.text: After the visit, you send the son a WhatsApp update about health and mood. Which role is this?
questions.explanation: Keeping the child informed after every visit is the Bridge to the child role.
